content: Lead poisoning continues to be one of the most prevalent and preventable environmental health issues affecting children, despite significant progress in the United States in reducing the number of children with elevated blood lead levels (BLLs). One of the goals of the Healthy People 2010 initiative is to eliminate blood lead levels exceeding 10 µg/dL among children nationwide. Children in the U.S. Refugee children, particularly those newly resettled, exhibit a significantly higher prevalence of elevated BLLs compared to the 2.2% prevalence observed in U.S. children. In New Hampshire, blood lead screening is mandated for newly arrived refugee children aged 6 months to 16 years. Starting in May 2004, 242 refugee children, primarily from Africa, were resettled in New Hampshire. Of these, 96 children underwent two rounds of BLL testing. The first blood samples were collected within 90 days of their arrival, and the second samples were taken 3 to 6 months after resettlement. Many of these children initially presented with capillary BLLs exceeding 10 µg/dL, with some cases ranging from 11 to 73 µg/dL. Additionally, five other children, who were siblings of these cases, also had elevated BLLs. Eleven families among the recently resettled group had at least one child with a BLL greater than 20 µg/dL. Environmental investigations identified moderate lead hazards in the children’s residences and lead-contaminated soil in play areas frequented by the children. Children with elevated BLLs also exhibited signs of severe chronic malnutrition. Pre-arrival health examinations revealed that 16 children (37.2%) suffered from severe growth retardation, as indicated by a Height-for-Age Z-score below -2, which corresponds to approximately the second percentile on standard pediatric growth curves. Among the 40 children for whom weight data was available, 10 (25%) showed evidence of either failure to gain weight or weight loss, as indicated by a Weight-for-Height Z-score below -2, also corresponding to approximately the second percentile. Recommendations for Primary Prevention of Elevated Blood Lead Levels: 1. Repeat BLL testing for all refugee children aged 6 months to 6 years, as well as for older children if clinically indicated, 3 to 6 months after they are placed in permanent residences, regardless of their initial test results. 2. Recognize that children who engage in pica behavior (mouthing or eating non-food items, such as soil) are at risk for lead poisoning, irrespective of the age of their housing. This behavior is particularly common in certain refugee populations. The New Hampshire case study highlights that while some children had elevated BLLs upon arrival in the U.S., the majority did not. However, follow-up testing conducted 60 to 90 days after their placement in permanent residences revealed elevated BLLs ranging from 11 to 72 µg/dL. Refugee children are typically eligible for Medicaid, the Women, Infants, and Children (WIC) program, and other social services for at least 8 months following resettlement, regardless of their family’s financial status.
